claims.text: The proposed initial material is a single-phase, near-random multi-component concentrated alloy with a baseline atomic-size mismatch.
Replacing a principal element with a chemically similar element of substantially different atomic radius can systematically change the alloy's atomic-size mismatch.
The proposed substitution can change atomic-size mismatch without changing phase stability or long-range chemical order.
Increasing atomic-size mismatch enhances local lattice distortion.
Local lattice distortions induce spatial fluctuations in stacking-fault or shear-fault energy.
Enhanced atomic-size mismatch produces heterogeneous local strain fields.
Enhanced atomic-size mismatch increases shear-fault energy in specific local regions.
Spatially heterogeneous strain or fault-energy regions act as pinning sites for dislocations.
The resulting rugged energy landscape raises activation barriers and lattice friction for dislocation motion.
Greater fault-energy fluctuations and stronger dislocation pinning increase yield strength.
Increasing atomic-size mismatch will increase yield strength relative to a lower-mismatch baseline.
Heterogeneous lattice strain increases strain hardening by creating pinning sites, increasing dislocation density, and promoting dislocation entanglement.
Changes in the local fault-energy landscape alter the selection of slip, faulting, and twinning pathways.
Reducing atomic-size mismatch will produce lower strength and less heterogeneous dislocation behavior.
The mechanism should govern behavior specifically when thermally activated dislocation motion predominates and phase transformation and short-range-order changes are minimized.
Activation energy for dislocation motion can be obtained directly through the proposed in situ TEM or diffraction observations.
A substitutional modified alloy and its baseline can have identical overall compositions while differing in atomic-size mismatch because one principal element has been replaced.
Failure to observe statistically significant increases in strength, activation barrier, or dislocation pinning in the higher-mismatch alloy would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention replaces one principal element, which changes elemental composition, while the baseline and experimental design require the compared alloys to have identical overall compositions. The intended invariant may be total principal-element concentration or equiatomicity, but that is not what is stated.
